title: Immersion testing: water paths, focusing, the bridge
goals: Set a water path long enough that the second interface echo lands beyond the back wall
Say why the gates are synchronised to the interface echo
Work out where a focused probe focuses inside the part
Work out the refracted angle in steel from a small tilt of the probe in water
Plan a raster scan on a bridge: index step, scan speed and how long it takes
summary:
In **immersion** testing the part and the probe sit in water; the probe never touches. Coupling is the same everywhere, nothing wears, and a **bridge** (gantry) moves the probe on X, Y and Z axes with a **gimbal** for its angle, all on encoders, so a computer can build a **C-scan** map.

The A-scan starts with the **interface echo** (front-surface echo) from the water–part boundary, at $t = \frac{2 WP}{v_w}$, with water at about **1480 m/s** (it rises about 3 m/s per °C).

Water to steel reflects about **88%** of the sound, so only about 12% goes in each way: expect to use much more gain than in contact testing.

**Water path rule**: sound also bounces back and forth in the water, giving a **second interface echo** at twice the first. It must arrive after the back-wall echo, or it sits among the real indications. So $WP > T \frac{v_w}{v_m}$: for steel, more than about a **quarter** of the thickness (plus a margin).

**Interface sync**: the gates are timed from the interface echo, not the initial pulse, so they stay on the same depths in the part when the surface is wavy or the water path changes.

**Normalising**: tilt the probe with the gimbal until the interface echo is at its highest: the beam is then square to the surface. A small tilt matters: by **Snell's law** ($\frac{\sin\theta_1}{v_1} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{v_2}$) a 5° tilt in water is about 20° in steel. The first critical angle, water to steel, is about 14.5°.

**Focused probes** concentrate the beam for better sensitivity and lateral resolution. Inside the part, the focus is pulled in: depth $\approx (F - WP)\frac{v_w}{v_m}$, about a quarter of the remaining water focal length in steel.

**Raster scan**: move along the scan axis, step along the index axis, repeat. The **index step** must be small enough that the beam covers the gaps (often half the beam width or less). Time ≈ (area ÷ index step) ÷ scan speed, plus turnarounds.

formulas.name: Interface echo time
formulas.says: The sound crosses the water to the part and back.
symbols: the time to the interface echo (s; µs on the screen)
the water path, probe face to part surface
the speed of sound in water, about 1480 m/s

formulas.name: Shortest water path
formulas.says: The water must take longer to cross than the part does, so the second interface echo comes after the back wall.
symbols: sound speed in the material (steel 5920 m/s)
formulas.example: 40 mm steel: $40 \times \frac{1480}{5920} = 10$ mm, so a water path of more than 10 mm (with margin, say 15).

formulas.name: Focus depth in the part
formulas.says: The focal length left over after the water is shortened by the ratio of the speeds when the beam enters the faster material.
symbols: the depth of the focus in the part (mm)
the probe's focal length in water (mm)
formulas.example: F = 100 mm, WP = 60 mm, steel: $(100 - 60) \times 0.25 = 10$ mm deep.

formulas.name: Snell's law
formulas.says: Going into a faster material, the beam bends away from the perpendicular, by the ratio of the speeds.
symbols: the angle in the water, from the perpendicular
the refracted angle in the part
formulas.example: 5° in water into steel: $\sin\theta_2 = 4 \times \sin 5^\circ = 0.349$, so about 20°.

bench.task: On an immersion tank you are trained and authorised to use, set up a 0° test on a flat steel or aluminium block of known thickness.
check: Wipe bubbles off the block and the probe face
Set a water path longer than a quarter of the thickness (steel), plus margin
Normalise: tilt the gimbal until the interface echo peaks
Find the second interface echo and check it lands beyond the back wall
Put a gate on the back wall, synchronised to the interface echo, and change the water path: the gate should stay on the back wall

cards.q: In an immersion test of 40 mm steel plates, with an 8 mm water path, an echo shows just before the back wall on every plate and everywhere you scan. What is it most likely to be?
options: The second interface echo: the water path is too short
A lamination running through every plate
cards.why: The water path's round trip in water (8 mm at 1480 m/s) takes about as long as 32 mm of steel's round trip. So the sound's second trip through the water lands at about 32 mm 'depth', every time. Lengthen the water path to more than a quarter of the thickness and it moves beyond the back wall.

cards.title: The set-up: water between probe and part
cards.body:
The part sits in a tank of water and the probe is held some way above it: the **water path** (WP). The water is the couplant, the same everywhere, and nothing rubs.

On the A-scan, after the initial pulse comes the **interface echo** (front-surface echo) from the water–part boundary, then echoes from inside, then the back wall.

Sound in water is slow, about **1480 m/s**, a quarter of steel's 5920 m/s:

$$t = \frac{2 WP}{v_w}$$
cards.more:
Compared with contact testing, the initial pulse and the part are pulled apart by the water. That has a bonus: the dead zone under the initial pulse is in the water, not in the part, so you can see much closer to the surface (the interface echo's own width is the limit now).

Numbers: 50 mm of water is $2 \times 0.050 \div 1480 = 67.6$ µs to the interface echo. 50 mm of steel would take only 16.9 µs.

Water speeds up as it warms, about 3 m/s per °C near room temperature, so a tank that warms through the day moves the interface echo slightly earlier.

cards.q: Sound travels at 1480 m/s in water. The water path is {wp} mm. When does the interface echo arrive?
cards.why: There and back through the water: twice the water path over the speed. mm ÷ (m/s) gives ms, so × 1000 for µs.

cards.title: Most of the sound stays out
cards.body:
Water and steel have very different **acoustic impedances** (density × sound speed). At the boundary, most of the sound reflects: water to steel sends back about **88%** and lets in only about **12%**, and the echo has to cross the boundary again on its way out.

So immersion needs much more **gain** than contact testing, and the interface echo is always the biggest thing on the screen.

See the split for water against different materials.
cards.more:
Impedance is how hard a material is to push sound through. Water is soft and light; steel is stiff and heavy: about 30 times the impedance. A wave hitting such a mismatch mostly bounces, like a ball against a wall.

With 12% in and 12% back out, the energy of an echo from inside is cut to about 1.4% before you even count the flaw's own reflection: about 18 dB less than if the boundary were not there. That is why immersion calibration is done in the water, on a reference block, never by copying contact settings.

Aluminium is a better match than steel, so a little more gets in.

cards.intro: Water is on the left. Pick a material for the part.

ask.q: For the material you picked, what percentage of the sound's intensity goes into the part?
ask.why: $T = 1 - R$, with $R = \left(\frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^2$. For your choice, {trans}% goes in. The bigger the mismatch, the less gets through.
ask.hint: Read the transmitted share, or work out R from the impedances and take it from 100%.

cards.title: The water path rule
cards.body:
Some sound bounces between the part and the probe and comes back again: a **second interface echo**, at twice the first one's time. If it lands before the back-wall echo, it sits among the real indications, on every part.

So the water must take longer to cross than the part does:

$$WP > T\frac{v_w}{v_m}$$

$T$ is the part's thickness, $v_m$ its sound speed. For **steel** that is more than about a **quarter** of the thickness; add a margin.
cards.more:
Time it. The back wall arrives one part-round-trip after the interface echo. The second interface echo arrives one water-round-trip after the first. For the second interface echo to come later, the water round trip must be the longer one.

Steel is four times faster than water (5920 against 1480), so a millimetre of water takes as long as four of steel. 40 mm of steel takes as long as 10 mm of water. With a 15 mm water path the second interface echo lands at about 60 mm steel-equivalent, safely past the 40 mm back wall.

For aluminium (6320 m/s) the factor is $\frac{1480}{6320} = 0.23$.

cards.q: A {th} mm steel plate (5920 m/s) is tested in water (1480 m/s). What is the shortest water path that keeps the second interface echo beyond the back wall?
cards.why: The water's round trip must outlast the steel's: thickness × the ratio of the speeds, about a quarter for steel. Use a margin above it in practice.
cards.hint: Water is about four times slower than steel.

cards.title: Gates synchronised to the interface
cards.body:
If the part's surface is wavy, tilted or curved, the water path changes as the probe moves, and every echo shifts in time with it.

So the gates are **synchronised to the interface echo** (an **IF gate** or interface trigger): the flaw gate starts a fixed time after the interface echo, not after the initial pulse. Then a gate set from 2 mm to 38 mm below the surface stays there, whatever the water path.

The interface gate must be set so it catches the interface echo, and nothing earlier, everywhere on the part.
cards.more:
Picture measuring a ceiling's height from a stepladder whose height keeps changing: you would measure from the floor you stand on, not from the bottom of the ladder.

Without sync: the probe moves over a dip 3 mm deep; the interface echo comes 4 µs later, and so does everything else. A gate fixed to the initial pulse slides up into the water or down past the back wall, and indications appear and vanish for no real reason.

With sync, the gate rides on the interface echo, so depth below the surface is what it measures. Most immersion systems also use the interface echo's time to keep the water path constant with the Z axis.

cards.q: Why are the flaw gates in an immersion scan timed from the interface echo rather than the initial pulse?
options: So they stay at the same depth in the part when the water path changes
So that the interface echo is never visible on the screen
Because the initial pulse is lost in the water
So the gain can be lower near the surface
cards.why: A change in water path (a wavy surface, a tilt) shifts every echo in time. Timed from the interface echo, the gates measure depth below the surface, which is what you want.

cards.title: Normalising, and what a small tilt does
cards.body:
For a straight (0°) test the beam must hit the surface **square on**. **Normalise** the probe: tilt it with the gimbal until the interface echo is at its **highest**.

Tilt matters more than it looks. Going from slow water into fast steel, the beam bends away from the perpendicular, by **Snell's law**:

$$\frac{\sin\theta_1}{v_1} = \frac{\sin\theta_2}{v_2}$$

Steel is 4 times faster, so a 5° tilt in water gives about 20° in steel. Past about **14.5°** in water (the **first critical angle**), no longitudinal wave enters steel at all: only a shear wave.
cards.more:
Light does the same going from air into water, the other way round: a straw looks bent. Sound going into a faster material bends away from the perpendicular, and the faster the material, the more.

Numbers: $\sin 5^\circ = 0.087$. Times 4 (5920 ÷ 1480): 0.349. The angle whose sine is 0.349 is 20.4°. A 1° wobble of the probe is about 4° in the steel, which can be the difference between a strong and a weak echo from a small flaw.

This is also a tool: tilting the probe on purpose (between about 15° and 27°) gives **shear waves** at 30° to 90° in steel, for angle-beam immersion tests.

cards.q: An immersion probe is tilted {a}° from the perpendicular in water (1480 m/s). At what angle does the longitudinal wave travel in steel (5920 m/s)?
cards.why: Snell's law: the sines go in the ratio of the speeds. Steel is 4 times faster than water, so the sine is 4 times bigger (not the angle itself, though for small angles it is nearly 4 times).

cards.title: Focused probes
cards.body:
An immersion probe can have a lens that **focuses** the beam to a narrow spot: more sensitivity to small flaws and sharper edges on a C-scan.

Its **focal length** $F$ is given **in water**. When the beam enters steel it bends, and the focus is pulled in towards the surface:

$$z \approx (F - WP)\frac{v_w}{v_m}$$

The focal length left after the water is cut to about a **quarter** in steel. To focus deeper, shorten the water path (but keep it above the water path rule).
cards.more:
A magnifying glass focuses sunlight to a spot at its focal length. Put a block of glass in the way and the spot moves: the light bends at the block's surface.

Numbers: a probe focused at 100 mm in water, set at 60 mm water path, has 40 mm of 'water focus' left when it meets the steel. In steel that becomes about $40 \times 0.25 = 10$ mm deep.

To focus at 20 mm deep in steel you need 80 mm of water-equivalent left, which a 100 mm probe cannot give with a sensible water path: choose a longer focal length. Focusing only helps near the focus; elsewhere the beam is wider than an unfocused one.

cards.q: A probe focuses at {fl} mm in water. The water path to steel is {wp} mm. Roughly how deep in the steel is the focus?
cards.why: The focal length left after the water is shortened by the speed ratio: about a quarter in steel.
cards.hint: Focal length left after the water path, times $\frac{1480}{5920}$.

cards.title: The bridge and the raster scan
cards.body:
The **bridge** is a gantry over the tank: **X** and **Y** axes across it, **Z** up and down, and a **gimbal** to tilt the probe. **Encoders** on each axis tell the computer where the probe is when each A-scan is taken.

A **raster scan** moves along the **scan axis**, steps along the **index axis**, comes back, and repeats. Each gate's peak amplitude (or time) at each point becomes a pixel: a **C-scan** map.

The **index step** must be small enough that the beam covers the strips in between: often half the beam width or less.

Time ≈ number of lines × line length ÷ scan speed, plus turnarounds.
cards.more:
It is like mowing a lawn in stripes: up, step over, back, step over. The width of each step must be less than the mower's width or you leave lines of grass.

Numbers: a 600 × 400 mm panel, 1 mm index, scanned along the 600 mm side at 250 mm/s. 400 lines × 600 mm = 240 000 mm of scanning; ÷ 250 = 960 s, 16 minutes, plus the turnarounds.

Halve the index step for finer detail and the time doubles. Scan faster and the pulse rate (PRF) must keep up: at 250 mm/s with a 1 mm pixel, 250 A-scans a second is the least it must give.

cards.q: A {sx} × {sy} mm part is raster scanned along its {sx} mm side at {v} mm/s, with an index step of {ix} mm. Ignoring turnarounds, how long does the scan take, in minutes?
cards.why: Each index step is one more line along the scan axis. Total distance ÷ speed is the time; the turnarounds add more in practice.
cards.hint: Number of lines = width ÷ index step. Each line is the length of the scan axis.

cards.q: Small dark spots appear on a C-scan of a clean panel, and they move when you wipe the panel. What are they?
cards.why: Bubbles on the surface reflect the sound before it gets in, so the points under them lose signal. Wipe the part (and the probe face) after it goes in, use clean, settled water, and a wetting agent if needed.

cards.q: The tank water warms by 5 °C through the day. What happens to the interface echo?
options: It does not move at all
cards.why: Sound in water speeds up by about 3 m/s per °C near room temperature, so the round trip through the water gets shorter. With the gates synchronised to the interface echo, depths in the part are not affected.

cards.q: Setting the water path for a 60 mm steel block. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: Add a margin for the second interface echo
Set the Z axis and check the second interface echo is past the back wall
cards.fix: Shortest water path: $60 \times \frac{1480}{5920} = 15$ mm, so set about 20 mm
cards.why: The ratio is upside down. Water is slower, so a short water path takes as long as a lot of steel: the water path is a quarter of the thickness, not four times it. Check on the screen: the second interface echo should land just past the back wall.

cards.q: An aluminium plate (6320 m/s) is {th} mm thick. What is the shortest water path (1480 m/s) that keeps the second interface echo beyond the back wall?
cards.why: Same rule, aluminium's speed: a little under a quarter of the thickness.

cards.q: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: The echo from the water–part surface
Tilting the probe until the interface echo peaks
How far the probe moves over between scan lines
A plan-view map of gate amplitude or time

cards.q: Compared with contact testing, why can immersion see flaws closer to the surface?
options: The initial pulse's dead zone falls in the water
Water makes the sound pulse longer
The interface echo cancels the initial pulse
cards.why: With water between probe and part, the initial pulse and its ringing are over long before the sound reaches the part. The limit is now the width of the interface echo, which a high-frequency focused probe keeps short.

cards.q: In immersion, with the gate synchronised to the interface echo, a flaw echo comes {dt} µs after the interface echo in steel (5920 m/s). How deep is the flaw?
cards.why: Timed from the interface, only the steel is in the path: the pulse-echo rule with steel's speed. Using water's speed here, or adding the water path, are the slips.
cards.hint: From the interface echo on, the sound is in steel: $d = \frac{vt}{2}$.

cards.q: You want to focus 15 mm deep in steel with a probe whose focal length in water is 75 mm. What water path?
cards.why: 15 mm in steel needs $15 \times 4 = 60$ mm of water focus left: $75 - 60 = 15$ mm of water path. Check the water path rule too: fine for a plate up to about 60 mm thick.

cards.q: On every part, an echo sits at a fixed place among the indications, and it moves when you change the water path. What is it?
options: A flaw common to every part
A bubble on the probe face
cards.why: It follows the water path, not the part: the sound's second trip through the water. Lengthen the water path until it lands beyond the back wall.

cards.q: Steel plate {th} mm thick. What is the minimum water path?
cards.why: A quarter of the thickness for steel; add a margin.

cards.q: Focal length {fl} mm in water, water path {wp} mm. Focus depth in steel?
cards.why: What is left of the focal length after the water, times about a quarter in steel.

cards.q: What keeps a flaw gate at the same depth below a wavy surface?
options: Timing it from the interface echo
Raising the gain on that channel
cards.why: Timed from the interface echo, the gate measures depth below the surface, wherever the surface is.
